claim: Breakdown of the specialized nuclear envelope in starfish oocytes is mediated by an Arp2/3-nucleated F-actin 'shell', in contrast to microtubule-driven tearing in mammalian fibroblasts.
source: We showed that breakdown of this specialized NE is mediated by an Arp2/3-nucleated F-actin 'shell' in starfish oocytes, in contrast to microtubule-driven tearing in mammalian fibroblasts.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' previous work (Mori et al., 2014) and contrasts with established mechanisms in mammalian cells (Beaudouin et al., 2002; Salina et al., 2002).

claim: Actin is nucleated within the lamina, sprouting filopodia-like spikes towards the nuclear membranes.
source: We show that actin is nucleated within the lamina, sprouting filopodia-like spikes towards the nuclear membranes.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data showing F-actin spikes extending from the lamina (Figure 3D, E) and EM data showing membrane protrusions with fibrous densities consistent with actin filaments (Figure 5D, E).

claim: F-actin spikes protrude pore-free nuclear membranes, whereas the adjoining stretches of membrane accumulate NPCs that are associated with the still-intact lamina.
source: These F-actin spikes protrude pore-free nuclear membranes, whereas the adjoining stretches of membrane accumulate NPCs that are associated with the still-intact lamina.
evidence: This is demonstrated by EM showing membrane spikes free of NPCs with NPC-dense regions at their base (Figure 5D, G), and STED imaging showing similar patterns (Figure 5G).

claim: Packed NPCs sort into a distinct membrane network, while breaks appear in ER-like, pore-free regions.
source: Packed NPCs sort into a distinct membrane network, while breaks appear in ER-like, pore-free regions.
evidence: This is supported by EM data showing NPC-dense nucleoplasmic bodies and rupture occurring in pore-free membrane regions (Figures 6, 7A).

claim: The nuclear envelope is composed of inner and outer nuclear membranes that are fused at nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) to mediate nucleo-cytoplasmic transport.
source: The nuclear envelope (NE), composed of inner and outer nuclear membranes, is a specialized sub-compartment of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) that separates the nucleus and the cytoplasm in eukaryotic cells. The inner and outer NE is fused at nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) to mediate nucleo-cytoplasmic transport.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nuclear envelope structure, supported by citation to Burke and Ellenberg, 2002.

claim: The lamina is a network of intermediate filaments that lines the nucleoplasmic side of the nuclear envelope and provides mechanical support.
source: This complex NE membrane structure is mechanically supported by a network of intermediate filaments, the lamina, which lines the nucleoplasmic side (Burke and Ellenberg, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about lamina structure and function, supported by citation.

claim: Oocytes have an exceptionally large nucleus known as the germinal vesicle.
source: Oocytes have a very specialized nuclear architecture with an exceptionally large nucleus, also known as the germinal vesicle, which stores nuclear components that are necessary to support early embryonic development.
evidence: This is established knowledge about oocyte nuclear structure.

claim: The oocyte nuclear envelope is densely packed with NPCs that serve as a stockpile for early embryonic development.
source: The oocyte NE is densely packed with NPCs that serve as a stockpile of these complexes (rendering oocytes a popular model in which to study NPCs), and the lamina is thick so that it is able to provide mechanical support for this very large structure (Goldberg and Allen, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goldberg and Allen, 1995, and is consistent with the EM data showing high NPC density (Figure 5A, B).

claim: In vertebrates and deuterostomes (including the echinoderm starfish), the complex NE structure is fully disassembled during division.
source: In Drosophila and Caenorhabditis elegans embryos, the NE and the lamina remains partially intact during cell division, whereas in vertebrates and deuterostomes (including the echinoderm starfish), the complex NE structure is fully disassembled during division.
evidence: This is established knowledge about differences in NE disassembly across species.

claim: In somatic mammalian cells, NE disassembly involves the complete dismantling of the NPCs, depolymerization of the lamina, and re-absorption of the nuclear membranes into the ER.
source: In somatic mammalian cells, NE disassembly involves the complete dismantling of the NPCs, depolymerization of the lamina, and re-absorption of the nuclear membranes into the ER (Hetzer, 2010; Ungricht and Kutay, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Hetzer, 2010 and Ungricht and Kutay, 2017.

claim: NEBD begins with a partial permeabilization of the NE resulting from phosphorylation-driven disassembly of the NPCs and other NE components.
source: In all species in which nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD) has been investigated in detail, including somatic cells and oocytes from various species, NEBD begins with a partial permeabilization of the NE resulting from phosphorylation-driven disassembly of the NPCs and other NE components (Dultz et al., 2008; Mühlhäusser and Kutay, 2007; Terasaki et al., 2001; Lénárt et al., 2003; Martino et al., 2017; Linder et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting this mechanism across species.

claim: During the first phase of NEBD, partial permeabilization allows proteins and smaller dextrans up to ~70 kDa to leak in or out of the nucleus.
source: This allows proteins, and smaller dextrans up to ~70 kDa, to leak in or out of the nucleus (Lénárt et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lénárt et al., 2003, and is consistent with the experimental use of 25 kDa dextran as a marker of partial permeabilization (Figure 4A, B).

claim: During the first phase of NEBD, the overall structure of the NE is still intact and the compartmentalization of large protein complexes is maintained.
source: Importantly, however, during this first phase of NEBD, the overall structure of the NE (as observed by electron microscopy (EM)) is still intact and the compartmentalization of large protein complexes (e.g. ribosomes and microtubules) is maintained (Terasaki et al., 2001; Lénárt et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Terasaki et al., 2001 and Lénárt et al., 2003.

claim: In cultured mammalian cells, microtubules tear the NE in a dynein-dependent process.
source: In cultured mammalian cells, microtubules tear the NE in a dynein-dependent process (Beaudouin et al., 2002; Salina et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beaudouin et al., 2002 and Salina et al., 2002.

claim: In the large oocyte nucleus, the actin cytoskeleton rather than the microtubule cytoskeleton is required for NE rupture.
source: By contrast, we have shown recently that in the large oocyte nucleus, the actin cytoskeleton rather than the microtubule cytoskeleton is required for NE rupture.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work (Mori et al., 2014) and the current data showing F-actin shell formation and its requirement for NE rupture (Figures 1, 2).

claim: A transient F-actin 'shell' is polymerized by the Arp2/3 complex on the inner surface of the NE and membranes undergo complete rupture within two minutes of its formation.
source: A transient F-actin 'shell' is polymerized by the Arp2/3 complex on the inner surface of the NE and membranes undergo complete rupture within two minutes of its formation (Mori et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mori et al., 2014 and the current live-cell imaging data (Figure 1A).

claim: The F-actin shell first appears as an equatorial band of foci when the NE is still intact and impermeable to large dextrans.
source: The F-actin shell first appears as an equatorial band of foci when the NE is still intact and impermeable to large dextrans (Figure 1A, 0 s).
evidence: This is directly observed in live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Approximately 30–45 s after the F-actin shell first appears, as the F-actin foci grow and intensify, merging to form a continuous F-actin shell, the first breaks on the NE appear, allowing a large 500 kDa dextran to flood into the nucleus.
source: Approximately 30–45 s later, as the F-actin foci grow and intensify, merging to form a continuous F-actin shell, the first breaks on the NE appear, allowing a large 500 kDa dextran to flood into the nucleus (Figure 1A, 45 s).
evidence: This is directly observed in live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The F-actin shell spreads towards the poles before a wave of membrane rupture takes place after a delay of ~30 s.
source: The shell then spreads towards the poles before a wave of membrane rupture takes place after a delay of ~30 s (Figure 1A, 90 s).
evidence: This is directly observed in live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: As the first F-actin foci began to assemble, the NE still appeared smooth and continuous.
source: When we looked at the process with our new approach, we saw that as the first F-actin foci began to assemble, the NE still appeared smooth and continuous, as visualized by a membrane probe (DiIC18(3)) and a marker of NPCs (a fragment of importin-β) (Figure 1B, −13 s).
evidence: This is directly observed in high-resolution live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 10–15 s after F-actin foci begin to assemble, the first spike-like membrane protrusions towards the cytoplasm are observed, which then rapidly escalate into a complex, convoluted and fragmented membrane structure.
source: 10–15 s later, we observed the first spike-like membrane protrusions towards the cytoplasm, which then rapidly escalated into a complex, convoluted and fragmented membrane structure (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is directly observed in high-resolution live-cell imaging data shown in Figures 1B-D.

claim: During membrane reorganization, NPCs appeared to separate partially from the membrane towards the nucleoplasmic side.
source: Intriguingly, during this process NPCs appeared to separate partially from the membrane towards the nucleoplasmic side.
evidence: This is observed in live-cell imaging data (Figure 1B) and confirmed by STED microscopy (Figure 3C).

claim: Dextran entry did not coincide with the formation of the initial membrane spikes, it occurred 20–30 s later, when membrane reorganization had progressed to a rather advanced stage.
source: Dextran entry did not coincide with the formation of the initial membrane spikes, it occurred 20–30 s later, when membrane reorganization had progressed to a rather advanced stage (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly observed in live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Membrane reorganization is dependent on actin assembly.
source: This membrane reorganization is dependent on actin assembly.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that inhibiting F-actin shell formation by depleting actin monomers prevents membrane reorganization (Figure 1E).

claim: If the F-actin shell is inhibited by injecting a large amount of the actin-binding UtrCH domain to deplete available actin monomers, the NE membrane stays smooth and continuous.
source: If the F-actin shell is inhibited by injecting a large amount of the actin-binding UtrCH domain to deplete available actin monomers, the NE membrane stays smooth and continuous (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Even when F-actin shell formation is inhibited, the nucleus does collapse and the NE ruffles and folds as a result of the progressing partial NE disassembly.
source: Even in this case, the nucleus does collapse and the NE ruffles and folds as a result of the progressing partial NE disassembly.
evidence: This is observed in experiments with UtrCH-mediated actin depletion (Figure 1E) and is consistent with previous work (Mori et al., 2014).

claim: When F-actin shell formation is inhibited, large and folded membrane fragments remain intact long after NEBD.
source: However, unlike in control oocytes, these large and folded membrane fragments remain intact long after NEBD, as we showed in earlier work (Mori et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Mori et al., 2014).

claim: In starfish oocytes, actin assembly mediates a reorganization of nuclear membranes that leads to NE rupture.
source: Thus, we concluded that, in starfish oocytes, actin assembly mediates a reorganization of nuclear membranes that leads to NE rupture.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the live-cell imaging data showing membrane reorganization dependent on F-actin assembly (Figures 1B-E).

claim: The endogenous lamin network remains continuous even minutes after NE rupture, although it folds and ruffles as the nucleus collapses during NEBD.
source: This confirmed our previous observations that the endogenous lamin network remains continuous even minutes after NE rupture, although it folds and ruffles as the nucleus collapses during NEBD (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly observed in immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B and is consistent with previous observations.

claim: The lamin mesh gradually coarsens during the process of NEBD.
source: In addition, imaging portions of the lamina en face by stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy suggests that the lamin mesh gradually coarsens during the process of NEBD (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed in STED microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The rupture of the NE does not proceed by F-actin-induced tearing or rapid disassembly of the lamina, which remains a continuous network throughout NEBD.
source: We conclude that the rupture of the NE does not proceed by F-actin-induced tearing or rapid disassembly of the lamina, which remains a continuous network throughout NEBD.
evidence: This conclusion is based on immunofluorescence and STED data showing continuous lamina throughout NEBD (Figure 2B).

claim: The lamina co-localized with phalloidin, while the NPC staining formed a separate layer of fragmented appearance up to 500 nm 'above' the F-actin shell.
source: We observed that although the lamina co-localized with phalloidin, the NPC staining formed a separate layer of fragmented appearance up to 500 nm 'above' the F-actin shell (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is directly observed in immunofluorescence data with line profile analysis shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The still-intact lamina appears to serve as the scaffold upon which the F-actin shell assembles, whereas the nuclear membranes appear to fragment and separate away from the lamina and the F-actin shell.
source: Thus, the still-intact lamina appears to serve as the scaffold upon which the F-actin shell assembles, whereas the nuclear membranes appear to fragment and separate away from the lamina and the F-actin shell.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization data showing lamina with F-actin and separation of NPCs/membranes (Figures 3A, B).

claim: Before NE rupture, the NPC and lamina stainings overlapped at the approx. 50 nm resolution afforded by STED, which is consistent with the known ultrastructure of the NE.
source: Before NE rupture, the NPC and lamina stainings overlapped at the approx. 50 nm resolution afforded by STED, which is consistent with the known ultrastructure of the NE (Figure 3C, pre-NEBD) (Burke and Ellenberg, 2002).
evidence: This is directly observed in STED data (Figure 3C) and is consistent with established knowledge (Burke and Ellenberg, 2002).

claim: At the shell stage, NPC-stained NE fragments 'float' above the intact lamina.
source: In stark contrast, at the shell stage, we were able to visualize NPC-stained NE fragments 'floating' above the intact lamina (Figure 3C, post-NEBD).
evidence: This is directly observed in STED data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The separation of lamina and membranes is dependent on the F-actin shell.
source: This separation of lamina and membranes is dependent on the F-actin shell, because this process did not occur when we prevented F-actin shell formation by inhibiting Arp2/3 using the small molecule inhibitor CK-666 (Figure 3C, post-NEBD + CK-666).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data using CK-666 inhibitor shown in Figure 3C.

claim: STED imaging of optimally fixed samples revealed filopodia-like F-actin spikes of 0.5–2 μm in length, spaced at ~0.1 μm, and extending from the base of the F-actin shell towards the nuclear membranes.
source: STED imaging of samples that were optimally fixed for phalloidin staining revealed filopodia-like F-actin spikes of 0.5–2 μm in length, spaced at ~0.1 μm, and extending from the base of the F-actin shell towards the nuclear membranes (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly observed and measured in STED microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex is localized at the base of the F-actin shell just beneath the NE, whereas the F-actin spikes extending from the base are not labeled by ArpC1.
source: Furthermore, using a starfish-specific anti-ArpC1 antibody, we localized the Arp2/3 complex at the base of the F-actin shell just beneath the NE, whereas the F-actin spikes extending from the base were not labeled by ArpC1 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is directly observed in STED microscopy data with ArpC1 antibody staining shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Membrane evaginations are largely free of NPCs, most probably because NPCs are still attached to the lamina, and thus NPCs are held back and cluster at the base of spikes.
source: Membrane evaginations are largely free of NPCs, most probably because NPCs are still attached to the lamina, and thus NPCs are held back and cluster at the base of spikes.
evidence: This is inferred from EM and STED data showing pore-free spikes with NPC clusters at their base (Figures 5D, G).

claim: The NE is smooth, continuous and is tightly packed with NPCs with a regular spacing of ~200 nm in immature oocytes, as well as in oocytes just before NE rupture and even in the intact polar regions of the NE undergoing rupture.
source: First, as consistent with earlier observations, the NE is smooth, continuous and is tightly packed with NPCs with a regular spacing of ~200 nm in immature oocytes, as well as in oocytes just before NE rupture and even in the intact polar regions of the NE undergoing rupture (see Figure 5A,B for image examples, and Figure 6C for quantification) (Lénárt et al., 2003).
evidence: This is directly observed in EM data (Figures 5A, B) with quantification (Figure 6C) and is consistent with previous observations (Lénárt et al., 2003).

claim: In areas closer to the rupture site, regions with gaps in NPC occupancy are observed, the number and size of which increased proximal to this region.
source: By contrast, in areas closer to the rupture site, we observed regions with gaps in NPC occupancy, the number and size of which increased proximal to this region (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly observed in EM data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the vicinity of the rupture site, gaps appeared to evolve into 'bumps' and membrane spikes.
source: In the vicinity of the site, gaps appeared to evolve into 'bumps' and membrane spikes (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is directly observed in EM data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The most prominent spikes observed rose ~1 µm above the level of the NE.
source: Although reconstructing the full 3D architecture of these spikes is challenging, even in 300-nm-thick tomographic sections, the most prominent spikes that we observed rose ~1 µm above the level of the NE (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is directly measured in EM and tomographic data shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Membrane spikes contain fibrous densities consistent with actin filaments.
source: These spikes contain fibrous densities consistent with actin filaments (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and are even more clearly distinguishable on tomographic reconstructions (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is directly observed in EM and tomographic data shown in Figure 5D, E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Membrane spikes observed by EM were covered by continuous nuclear membranes and almost completely free of NPCs.
source: Intriguingly, on both thin sections and tomographic reconstructions, we observed that these spikes were covered by continuous nuclear membranes and almost completely free of NPCs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is directly observed in EM and tomographic data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Pore-free areas pushed out by the F-actin shell are surrounded by NPC-dense adjacent regions.
source: These pore-free areas are surrounded by NPC-dense adjacent regions (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is directly observed in EM data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: NPC-free areas pushed out by the F-actin shell may cause the crowding of NPCs in juxtaposed regions.
source: We are unable to estimate the 3D membrane areas from 2D sections, nevertheless, our data suggest that NPC-free areas pushed out by the F-actin shell may cause the crowding of NPCs in juxtaposed regions (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is inferred from EM observations and quantification of NPC spacing shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The lamina runs at the base of the F-actin shell, below but still attached to NPC clusters.
source: In addition, we were able to visualize that the lamina runs at the base of the F-actin shell, below but still attached to NPC clusters, suggesting that NPCs might be held back at the base of spikes by their attachments to the lamina (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is directly observed in STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: NPCs might be held back at the base of spikes by their attachments to the lamina.
source: In addition, we were able to visualize that the lamina runs at the base of the F-actin shell, below but still attached to NPC clusters, suggesting that NPCs might be held back at the base of spikes by their attachments to the lamina (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is inferred from STED microscopy data showing lamina at the base of F-actin shell with attached NPC clusters (Figure 5G).

claim: The growing gaps between NPCs develop into bumps and spikes that are protrusions generated by Arp2/3-driven actin polymerization, which pries nuclear membranes and lamina apart.
source: Together, our data from EM correlated with live cell and immunofluorescence suggest that the growing gaps between NPCs, which then develop into bumps and spikes, are protrusions generated by Arp2/3-driven actin polymerization, which pries nuclear membranes and lamina apart.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including EM, live-cell imaging, and immunofluorescence (Figures 3, 5).

claim: In regions closer to rupture sites, an increasing segregation of pore-free and pore-dense segments is observed.
source: In regions closer to rupture sites, we observed an increasing segregation of pore-free and pore-dense segments (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly observed in EM data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Nucleoplasmic bodies are dense, round structures 200–500 nm in diameter beneath the NE in the nucleoplasm.
source: Furthermore, accompanying spikes and NPC-rich clusters, we observed additional frequent membrane structures, which we call nucleoplasmic bodies. These are dense, round structures 200–500 nm in diameter beneath the NE in the nucleoplasm (Figures 5D and 6B).
evidence: This is directly observed and measured in EM data shown in Figures 5D and 6B.

claim: Nucleoplasmic bodies often appear in a beads-on-a-string arrangement with a slightly electron-denser material connecting them.
source: These bodies often appear in a beads-on-a-string arrangement with a slightly electron-denser material connecting them (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is directly observed in EM data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Above nucleoplasmic bodies, the NE appears to be still intact, consisting mostly of NPC-free nuclear membranes and maintaining the nucleo-cytoplasmic boundary, as judged by the distribution of ribosomes.
source: Above them, the NE appears to be still intact, consisting mostly of NPC-free nuclear membranes and maintaining the nucleo-cytoplasmic boundary, as judged by the distribution of ribosomes.
evidence: This is directly observed in EM data (Figure 6B) based on ribosome distribution.

claim: In pore-dense segments and nucleoplasmic bodies, pore-to-pore distance decreased substantially from ~200 nm in intact areas to ~100 nm.
source: In pore-dense segments, as well as in nucleoplasmic bodies, our quantification shows that pore-to-pore distance decreased substantially from ~200 nm in intact areas to ~100 nm (Figure 6C), suggesting that the NPC-free membranes are generated by redistribution of NPCs.
evidence: This is directly measured and quantified from EM data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: NPC-free membranes are generated by redistribution of NPCs.
source: In pore-dense segments, as well as in nucleoplasmic bodies, our quantification shows that pore-to-pore distance decreased substantially from ~200 nm in intact areas to ~100 nm (Figure 6C), suggesting that the NPC-free membranes are generated by redistribution of NPCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantification of NPC spacing showing increased density in some regions and decreased density in others (Figure 6C).

claim: Nucleoplasmic bodies may form by invagination of NPC-rich clusters, initially inducing pits that curve into the nucleoplasm and then forming inverted NE tubules filled inside with cytoplasm.
source: Careful examination of intermediates suggests that nucleoplasmic bodies may form by invagination of NPC-rich clusters, initially inducing pits that curve into the nucleoplasm and then forming inverted NE tubules filled inside with cytoplasm (Figure 6A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from examination of EM intermediates shown in Figures 6A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The electron density along the boundary of nucleoplasmic bodies corresponds to closely juxtaposed NPCs with an intact central ring structure, similar to NPCs in still-intact areas.
source: Sections capturing these structures en face and tomograms confirm that the electron density along the boundary of the bodies corresponds to closely juxtaposed NPCs with an intact central ring structure, similar to NPCs in still-intact areas (see 'nucleoplasmic bodies' in Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is directly observed in EM sections and tomograms shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: The membranes were interrupted in areas where the segregation of pore-dense and pore-free regions was strongest and NPC invaginations frequent and most dramatic.
source: Finally, the EM montages revealed that the membranes were interrupted in areas where the segregation of pore-dense and pore-free regions was strongest and NPC invaginations frequent and most dramatic (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is directly observed in EM montages shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In areas of membrane rupture, no continuous membrane boundary was seen to separate cyto- and nucleoplasm, but nucleoplasmic bodies were abundant.
source: Here, no continuous membrane boundary was seen to separate cyto- and nucleoplasm, but nucleoplasmic bodies were abundant.
evidence: This is directly observed in EM data (Figure 7A).

claim: Light microscopy of the stage corresponding to membrane rupture revealed a complex tubular-vesicular network that was densely labeled by NPC staining.
source: Light microscopy of the corresponding stage revealed a complex tubular-vesicular network that was densely labeled by NPC staining, occasionally resolving cross-sections of tubules consistent with our EM data (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is directly observed in STED microscopy data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: NE rupture proceeds by F-actin-driven sorting of NE membranes into pore-dense and pore-free segments.
source: Together, our data show that NE rupture proceeds by F-actin-driven sorting of NE membranes into pore-dense and pore-free segments.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple lines of evidence from EM, live-cell imaging, and immunofluorescence showing membrane segregation (Figures 5, 6, 7).

claim: Pore-dense segments invaginate, forming a network of nucleoplasmic bodies, whereas rupture occurs in evaginating pore-free segments.
source: Pore-dense segments invaginate, forming a network of nucleoplasmic bodies, whereas rupture occurs in evaginating pore-free segments.
evidence: This conclusion is based on EM data showing invaginating NPC-dense regions and rupture in pore-free regions (Figures 6, 7).

claim: F-actin foci form within the lamina when cytoplasmic components, such as the Arp2/3 complex and actin monomers, reach a critical concentration in the nucleus as a result of the gradual, phosphorylation-driven disassembly and increasing leakiness of the NPCs in the first phase of NEBD.
source: We hypothesize that these foci form at the time when cytoplasmic components, such as the Arp2/3 complex and actin monomers, reach a critical concentration in the nucleus as a result of the gradual, phosphorylation-driven disassembly and increasing leakiness of the NPCs in the first phase of NEBD.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known mechanism of NPC disassembly and the observed timing of F-actin foci formation.

claim: Once triggered, F-actin foci grow rapidly, which is expected as a result of the autocatalytic nature of Arp2/3-mediated nucleation of branched F-actin networks.
source: Once triggered, F-actin foci grow rapidly, which is expected as a result of the autocatalytic nature of Arp2/3-mediated nucleation of branched F-actin networks.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Arp2/3-mediated actin polymerization and is consistent with the observed rapid growth of F-actin foci (Figure 1A).

claim: The filaments seem to grow preferentially from the shell base in the lamina towards nuclear membranes, and push against them.
source: As the foci spread, they merge to form a continuous shell. The filaments seem to grow preferentially from the shell base in the lamina towards nuclear membranes, and push against them.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed morphology of F-actin spikes extending from the lamina towards membranes (Figures 3D, 5D, E).

claim: The asymmetry in filament growth may be explained by the fact that force imposed on actin filaments promotes the nucleation of a branched meshwork.
source: This asymmetry may be explained by the fact that force imposed on actin filaments promotes the nucleation of a branched meshwork (Bieling et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on established knowledge from Bieling et al., 2016.

claim: F-actin networks that are nucleated in vitro on micropatterned activated Arp2/3 show a morphology that is strikingly similar to that of the F-actin shell, with filopodia-like bundles pointing away from a base of dense branched network.
source: Intriguingly, F-actin networks that are nucleated in vitro on micropatterned activated Arp2/3 show a morphology that is strikingly similar to that of the F-actin shell, with filopodia-like bundles pointing away from a base of dense branched network (Reymann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reymann et al., 2010.

claim: Localized activation of Arp2/3 within the lamina may be sufficient to explain the morphology of the F-actin shell.
source: This suggests that localized activation of Arp2/3 within the lamina may be sufficient to explain the morphology of the F-actin shell.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity to in vitro F-actin networks (Reymann et al., 2010) and the observed localization of Arp2/3 at the base of the shell (Figure 3E).

claim: The F-actin shell protrudes pore-free nuclear membranes, separating these from the lamina, because most NPCs are attached to the still-intact lamina at this stage, and thus are held back, while membranes are protruded by actin assembly.
source: Our light and electron microscopy data clearly show that the F-actin shell protrudes pore-free nuclear membranes, separating these from the lamina. We propose that these membranes are cleared of NPCs, because most NPCs are attached to the still-intact lamina at this stage, and thus are held back, while membranes are protruded by actin assembly.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on EM and light microscopy data showing pore-free membrane protrusions with NPCs remaining at the base attached to lamina (Figures 5, 6).

claim: As the NPCs accumulate between pore-free spikes, the membranes in these NPC-rich dimples buckle into the nucleoplasm and invaginate to form nucleoplasmic bodies.
source: Then, as the NPCs accumulate between pore-free spikes, the membranes in these NPC-rich dimples buckle into the nucleoplasm and invaginate to form nucleoplasmic bodies.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on EM data showing NPC-rich invaginations forming nucleoplasmic bodies (Figures 6A, B).

claim: Pore-free nuclear membranes that are separated from the lamina are unstable, and thus rupture and rearrange into an ER-like reticular structure.
source: Our data suggest that pore-free nuclear membranes that are separated from the lamina are unstable, and thus rupture and rearrange into an ER-like reticular structure.
evidence: This is inferred from EM data showing rupture occurring in pore-free regions (Figure 7A).

claim: Detaching the nuclear membranes from the lamin network leads to NE rupture in various physiological contexts.
source: However, in agreement with our model, it has been shown in various other physiological contexts that detaching the nuclear membranes from the lamin network leads to NE rupture.
evidence: This is supported by examples from cancer cells and micronuclei (Hatch et al., 2013) and migrating cells (Thiam et al., 2016; Davidson and Lammerding, 2014; Denais et al., 2016).

claim: NE rupture frequently occurs in cancer cells, in particular in micronuclei, where breaching of the NE barrier is preceded by local lamin disruption.
source: For example, NE rupture frequently occurs in cancer cells, in particular in micronuclei, where breaching of the NE barrier is preceded by local lamin disruption (Hatch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hatch et al., 2013.

claim: The 'breakability' of the nucleus in migrating cells is dependent on lamin composition.
source: Recent work shows that the 'breakability' of the nucleus in migrating cells is dependent on lamin composition (Thiam et al., 2016; Davidson and Lammerding, 2014; Denais et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thiam et al., 2016; Davidson and Lammerding, 2014; and Denais et al., 2016.

claim: In somatic cells, NEBD proceeds by microtubule-mediated tearing of the lamina.
source: Indeed, in somatic cells, it has been shown that NEBD proceeds by microtubule-mediated tearing of the lamina (Beaudouin et al., 2002; Salina et al., 2002), but the precise morphology of the NE intermediates at a resolution comparable to that which we achieved in starfish oocytes is not known.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beaudouin et al., 2002 and Salina et al., 2002.

claim: A mechanism based on the segregation of lamina, NPCs and membranes may play a critical role in destabilizing the NE during NE rupture in somatic cells.
source: Therefore, it is possible that a similar mechanism, based on the segregation of lamina, NPCs and membranes, plays a critical role in destabilizing the NE during NE rupture in somatic cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the mechanism observed in starfish oocytes and the lack of detailed structural information for somatic cells.

claim: F-actin assembly may facilitate NE rupture by increasing membrane tension in evaginations, or by causing extreme membrane curvatures at the boundary of invaginations.
source: F-actin assembly may facilitate this process by increasing membrane tension in evaginations, or by causing extreme membrane curvatures, for example at the boundary of invaginations, thereby facilitating NE rupture or possibly complete NPC disassembly.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism by which F-actin assembly leads to membrane rupture.

claim: The ESCRT machinery may be involved in membrane rearrangements during NEBD.
source: In addition, although this hypothesis remains rather speculative at this point, it is intriguing to consider links between our work and what has been shown for repair of interphase NE rupture, as well as reassembly of NE after division, both instances involving the ESCRT machinery (Denais et al., 2016; Raab et al., 2016; Olmos et al., 2015). In our NEBD intermediates, we observe membrane topologies that are similar to those involved in NE repair, suggesting that the ESCRT complex may also be involved in these membrane rearrangements.
evidence: This is speculation based on similarities in membrane topology to processes known to involve ESCRT (Denais et al., 2016; Raab et al., 2016; Olmos et al., 2015).

claim: An F-actin shell similar to that in starfish oocytes has been observed in several species, including other echinoderm species such as sea urchin, the cnidarian model Nematostella vectensis, and polychaete worms.
source: Intriguingly, an F-actin shell similar to that in starfish oocytes has been observed in several species, although these structures are yet to be characterized in detail. These species include other echinoderm species, such as sea urchin (Burkel et al., 2007), the cnidarian model Nematostella vectensis (DuBuc et al., 2014), and polychaete worms (Jacobsohn, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burkel et al., 2007; DuBuc et al., 2014; and Jacobsohn, 1999.

claim: F-actin-mediated NE rupture may be widely spread across animal species.
source: These examples strongly suggest that F-actin-mediated NE rupture may be widely spread across animal species, and we speculate that the presence or absence of this mechanism may be correlated with differences in NE disassembly dynamics, nuclear size and other differences in physiology.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of F-actin shells in multiple species (Burkel et al., 2007; DuBuc et al., 2014; Jacobsohn, 1999).

claim: The clearing of NPCs off the membrane during NEBD appears to be conserved in organisms with partially open mitosis.
source: Finally, the clearing of NPCs off the membrane during NEBD appears to be conserved in organisms with partially open mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by examples from Ustilago maydis and Schizosaccharomyces japonicus (Straube et al., 2005; Aoki et al., 2011; Theisen et al., 2008).

claim: In Ustilago maydis, tearing of the NE is caused by microtubules pulling the nucleus through a small opening into the bud of the daughter cell.
source: Tearing of the NE has been observed in the fungus Ustilago maydis and the yeast Schizosaccharomyces japonicus. In U. maydis, the shearing is caused by microtubules pulling the nucleus through a small opening into the bud of the daughter cell (Straube et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Straube et al., 2005.

claim: Schizosaccharomyces japonicus splits the NE by stretching the nucleus between the two poles of a dividing cell.
source: Sz. japonicus, on the other hand, splits the NE by stretching the nucleus between the two poles of a dividing cell (Aoki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aoki et al., 2011.

claim: Schizosaccharomyces japonicus redistributes the NPCs to the two poles, freeing naked membranes at the NE regions destined to be broken.
source: Thus, NE rupture occurs by different means, but intriguingly, both show evidence of clearing NPCs before the NE is torn: Sz. japonicus redistributes the NPCs to the two poles, freeing naked membranes at the NE regions destined to be broken.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aoki et al., 2011.

claim: NPCs of Ustilago maydis initiate release of nucleoporins prior to rupture just as in higher eukaryotes.
source: NPCs of U. maydis on the other hand initiate release of nucleoporins prior to rupture just as in higher eukaryotes (Straube et al., 2005; Aoki et al., 2011; Theisen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Straube et al., 2005; Aoki et al., 2011; and Theisen et al., 2008.

claim: The F-actin shell destabilizes the NE by segregating pore-dense and pore-free membranes, providing the first mechanistic explanation for the sudden collapse of the NE structure during its breakdown.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that the F-actin shell destabilizes the NE by segregating pore-dense and pore-free membranes, providing the first mechanistic explanation for the sudden collapse of the NE structure during its breakdown.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the presented data.

claim: The mechanism of F-actin-mediated NE rupture is likely to function in many animal species.
source: As discussed above, this mechanism is likely to function in many animal species.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar F-actin structures in multiple species (Burkel et al., 2007; DuBuc et al., 2014; Jacobsohn, 1999).

claim: The segregation of nuclear membranes from the lamin network appears to be a general feature of nuclear rupture observed in dividing mammalian somatic cells, as well as during the interphase NE rupture that is frequent in cancer cells.
source: In other species, forces may be generated by means other than Arp2/3-mediated actin polymerization, but the segregation of nuclear membranes from the lamin network appears to be a general feature of nuclear rupture observed in dividing mammalian somatic cells, as well as during the interphase NE rupture that is frequent in cancer cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism observed in starfish oocytes and examples from other systems (Hatch et al., 2013; Thiam et al., 2016; Davidson and Lammerding, 2014; Denais et al., 2016).

claim: The stage when the 25-kDa dextran almost completely fills the nucleus but the large, 160-kDa dextran is still excluded identifies the time-window of F-actin shell formation and NE rupture.
source: Thus, the stage when the 25-kDa dextran almost completely fills the nucleus but the large, 160-kDa dextran is still excluded identifies the time-window of F-actin shell formation and NE rupture.
evidence: This is based on the known permeability properties of the NE during NEBD (Lénárt et al., 2003) and is used as a staging criterion for EM samples (Figure 4A, B).

claim: NE rupture initiates near the 'equator' of the nucleus and spreads as a wave towards the poles.
source: The montage illustrates the key advantage of the system, which allows the progression of NE rupture to be observed spatially ordered on a single section of the large oocyte nucleus. The arrangement of the rupture site is fully consistent with the live and fixed light microscopy data: NE rupture initiates near the 'equator' of the nucleus and spreads as a wave towards the poles (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly observed in EM montages (Figure 4C) and is consistent with live and fixed light microscopy data (Figures 1A, 2A, 4D).
